The effects of this study are detailed in section 3. The quality of evidence was downgraded from high to low because of a serious risk of bias and significant imprecision. 2. One longitudinal study was included in the analysis. The evidence was not downgraded as the study was determined to have a low risk of bias. This criterion was not applicable in this case. 3. The evidence was downgraded because only one study was included in the analysis. The effects of this study are detailed in section 4. The quality of evidence was further downgraded from low to very low due to serious imprecision. 4. Four randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were included in the analysis, with a total of 326 participants. The evidence was downgraded by one level because 75% (3 out of 4) of the studies had a PEDro score below 6/10. However, the evidence was not downgraded due to heterogeneity, as most comparisons (16 out of 18) demonstrated a positive effect. Since the included studies were similar in terms of population, intervention, comparator, and outcome, the evidence was not downgraded based on this criterion. The effects of each individual study are detailed in section 5. The quality of evidence was downgraded from high to low due to a serious risk of bias and significant imprecision. 5. Two RCTs were included in the analysis, with a total of 204 participants. The evidence was downgraded by one level because 50% (1 out of 2) of the studies had a PEDro score below 6/10. The evidence was not downgraded due to heterogeneity, as all comparisons (4 out of 4) demonstrated a positive effect. The effects of each individual study are detailed in section 6. The quality of evidence was downgraded from high to low due to a serious risk of bias and significant imprecision. 6. The systematic review by Binkley and Rudd (2019) investigated the effects of head-out aquatic exercise (AE) on physiological and psychological outcomes in healthy postmenopausal women aged 50–70 years. Fifteen studies were reviewed, showing variability in interventions and assessments. Outcomes included inconclusive results for anthropometric measures (e.g., BMI, body fat), improvements in upper and lower body strength, flexibility, functional movements (e.g., walking, balance), bone density, and quality of life. Biochemical and hormonal variables were inconclusive. The authors concluded that head-out AE is effective for improving strength, flexibility, functional movements, bone density, and quality of life in postmenopausal women. 7. Bruderer-Hofstetter et al. (2018) conducted a systematic review and network meta-analysis to evaluate multicomponent interventions (MCTs) combining physical and cognitive training in elderly individuals with normal cognition (NC) or mild cognitive impairment (MCI). The analysis included 17 studies (6 with MCI, 11 with NC). Five MCTs were found to be superior to physical or cognitive training alone for improving physical capacity and/or cognitive function, but none improved instrumental activities of daily living (IADL). MCTs performed separately or simultaneously were effective in NC individuals, while separate MCTs were more effective in MCI individuals. The authors emphasized the need for a framework to design MCTs that effectively improve IADL. 8. Bueno de Souza et al. (2018) conducted a meta-analysis to examine the effects of mat Pilates on physical functional performance in older adults. Nine RCTs met the inclusion criteria, with five studies demonstrating high methodological quality. Mat Pilates was found to improve dynamic balance, lower limb strength, hip and lower back flexibility, and cardiovascular endurance in older adults. The authors recommended further high-quality studies to clarify the effects of mat Pilates on other physical functional measures in this population. 9. Burton et al. (2019) reviewed the effectiveness of physical activity programs for older adults receiving home care services. Eighteen studies, including ten RCTs, were analyzed. The meta-analysis showed limited evidence for the effectiveness of physical activity interventions in this population. The authors suggested that future studies should focus solely on physical improvements and include process evaluations to better understand the relationship between adherence and intervention effectiveness. 10. Da Rosa Orssatto et al. (2019) conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to compare the effects of fast-intended-velocity versus moderate-velocity resistance training on functional capacity in older adults. Fifteen studies were included, but the evidence was inconclusive regarding the superiority of fast-intended-velocity training. The results were influenced by a lack of high-quality studies, high heterogeneity, and publication bias. The authors highlighted the need for more rigorous research to determine the optimal resistance training velocity for improving functional capacity. 11. De Souto Barreto et al. (2019) systematically reviewed the association of long-term exercise interventions (≥1 year) with the risk of falls, fractures, hospitalizations, and mortality in older adults. Thirty-nine RCTs were included, with multicomponent training (e.g., aerobic, strength, balance) being the most common intervention. Long-term exercise was associated with reduced falls, injurious falls, and possibly fractures, but not with multiple falls, hospitalizations, or mortality. Meta-regressions suggested that exercising 2–3 times per week is optimal. The authors concluded that long-term exercise benefits older adults, including those with cardiometabolic and neurological conditions. 12. Dillon et al. (2018) reviewed exercise-based fall prevention strategies in adults aged 50+ with visual impairment. Seven RCTs were included, with three new trials added to the original review. The analysis aimed to determine the impact of exercise on fall prevention and physical function in this population. Results from the updated review are pending further elaboration.
